title: JustWatch, which tackles streaming fragmentation, launches own streaming service

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: Two students discuss a media studies assignment on how niche streaming services attract subscribers.

script.en: You look glued to your laptop. Are you still trying to map out that media studies assignment on niche streaming platforms?
Exactly. I'm comparing two small services, and the puzzle is why anyone would pay for a library that looks so thin when the big platforms have thousands of titles.
That's the interesting part. I read a case study suggesting that limited libraries can actually work if the service owns rights to films that are hard to find elsewhere.
So the advantage isn't volume but exclusivity. That would explain why one of the services I'm looking at charges only four dollars a month and still advertises a growing subscriber base.
Right. And some of them offer a lifetime deal for around fifty dollars, though my source said that kind of offer is usually time-limited.
That's a clever marketing hook. It lowers the barrier for people who hate recurring charges, but it also means the company gets cash upfront to buy more content later.
Did your case study mention how these services use audience data? I remember something about first-party data helping studios target ads more precisely.
Yes, and that seems to be the real business model. The streaming app collects viewing habits, and the parent company sells that insight to distributors planning marketing campaigns.
So the subscription fee may matter less than the data. That changes how I should frame my conclusion.
Me too. I was going to argue that small libraries are a weakness, but now I think the weakness is deliberate—it signals a curated catalogue rather than a random collection.
Careful, though. The professor warned us not to overgeneralise from one case. We should note that the strategy depends on having exclusive rights and a parent company with an ad business.
Fair point. I'll present it as a conditional advantage rather than a universal rule. Thanks—that saves me from a shaky argument.

sections.title: Passage
sections.scene: A monologue on how streaming platforms use audience data to reshape advertising.

script.en: When streaming services first appeared, many observers assumed that their main product was entertainment. Subscribers paid a monthly fee, watched films and series, and the business model seemed straightforward. Over the past decade, however, a quieter shift has taken place. Streaming platforms have become valuable not only because of what they show but because of what they learn about the people watching. Every time a viewer pauses a film, abandons a series after two episodes, or returns to a favourite title, the platform records a signal. Individually, these signals seem trivial, and collected across millions of users, they form a detailed picture of taste, habit and intention. This is what industry analysts call first-party audience data, and it is increasingly central to how media companies make money. The commercial logic is easy to follow. A studio planning a marketing campaign wants to know which audiences are likely to respond. Instead of relying on broad demographic categories, it can use viewing patterns to target advertisements more precisely. A platform that both streams content and sells advertising space therefore occupies a strategic position: it controls the content that attracts viewers and the data that explains them. This does not mean that subscription fees are irrelevant. They remain an important source of revenue, especially for services without a large advertising business. But the relative importance of fees may decline as data-driven advertising grows. Some smaller services have even launched with modest libraries, apparently betting that a narrow but distinctive catalogue will attract a loyal audience whose behaviour is easier to measure. The trend raises questions that go beyond business strategy. If platforms know more about viewers than viewers know about themselves, the balance of power in media may shift further toward those who control the data. For audiences, the convenience of personalised recommendations comes with a less visible cost: the gradual transformation of private viewing habits into a commercial asset.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How streaming platforms turn viewer data into commercial value

sections.title: When Streaming Guides Become Streaming Services
sections.passage:
JustWatch began in 2015 as a search engine for streaming content, helping users locate films across an expanding array of platforms. Its core promise was simple: tell people where a title is available and let them decide which service to pay for. That promise, however, has gradually been complicated by the company's own ambition. This month JustWatch launched its own streaming service, JustWatch TV, signalling a shift from neutral guide to commercial participant.

The new service offers a small catalogue of films free with advertisements, including titles that are not freely available elsewhere. A paid subscription, currently four dollars a month or fifty dollars for a lifetime, removes the ads. Company representatives describe the library as containing a few hundred titles across different tiers, supplied by about thirty content partners. By the standards of major platforms, the collection is modest and somewhat dated.

That modesty may be deliberate. A narrow catalogue built around hard-to-find films can attract viewers who value curation over volume. Roku's Howdy, a comparable service with a limited library, reportedly reached one million subscribers within six months of launch. The lesson is not that small libraries always succeed, but that exclusivity and low prices can create a viable niche when the target audience is clearly defined.

The more significant development lies behind the screen. JustWatch already operates an advertising business that uses first-party audience data from its streaming guide to help studios and distributors plan campaigns. By adding its own streaming service, the company can observe viewing behaviour directly rather than infer it from search queries. This deeper data, it argues, will improve targeting for clients across digital platforms. The subscription fee, in other words, may be less important than the information the service generates.

For users, the arrangement offers convenience and a degree of choice. Yet it also blurs a boundary that once seemed clear. A guide that recommends where to watch is expected to serve the viewer's interest; a service that sells advertising and data has an interest of its own. JustWatch insists that its vision is to direct fans to all their entertainment options in one place. Whether a company can remain a trusted guide while also competing in the market it once merely mapped is a question the next few years will answer.

long_sentences.en: “[JustWatchTV] will provide even deeper audience data and insights for JustWatch Media, the group’s campaign planning and buying service for film marketing campaigns across digital platforms like YouTube, Meta, and TikTok for studios, distributors, streamers, and media agencies,” the announcement said.

“From the beginning, our vision was to create a single platform that directs fans to all of their entertainment options in one place,” David Croyé, founder and CEO of JustWatch Group, said in a statement.

“JustWatch TV will help fill in the gaps and will make it easier for the massive JustWatch audience to discover and watch great movies and series, including those hard-to-find titles, right from the app itself.”
